In [[multilinear algebra]], a '''reshaping''' of [[Tensor (intrinsic definition)#Definition via tensor products of vector spaces|tensors]] is any [[bijection]] between the set of [[indexed family|indices]] of an [[Tensor order|order]]-<math>M</math> tensor and the set of indices of an order-<math>L</math> tensor, where <math>L < M </math>.  The use of indices presupposes tensors in coordinate representation with respect to a basis.  The coordinate representation of a tensor can be regarded as a multi-dimensional array, and a bijection from one set of indices to another therefore amounts to a rearrangement of the array elements into an array of a different shape.  Such a rearrangement constitutes a particular kind of [[linear map]] between the vector space of order-<math>M</math> tensors and the vector space of order-<math>L</math> tensors.

== Definition ==
Given a positive integer <math>M</math>, the notation <math>[M]</math> refers to the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>\{1, \dots, M \}</math> of the first {{mvar|M}} positive integers.

For each integer <math>m</math> where <math>1 \le m \le M </math> for a positive integer <math>M</math>, let <math>V_m</math> denote an <math>I_m</math>-[[Dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[vector space]] over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] <math>F</math>. Then there are vector space isomorphisms (linear maps)

<math display="block">\begin{align}
V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_M 
& \simeq F^{I_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_M} \\
& \simeq F^{I_{\pi_1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_{\pi_M}} \\
& \simeq F^{I_{\pi_1} I_{\pi_2}} \otimes F^{I_{\pi_3}} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_{\pi_M}} \\
& \simeq F^{I_{\pi_1} I_{\pi_3}} \otimes F^{I_{\pi_2}} \otimes F^{I_{\pi_4}} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_{\pi_M}} \\
& \,\,\,\vdots \\
& \simeq F^{I_1 I_2 \ldots I_M},
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_M</math> is any [[permutation]] and <math>\mathfrak{S}_M </math> is the [[symmetric group]] on <math>M</math> elements.  Via these (and other) vector space isomorphisms, a tensor can be interpreted in several ways as an order-<math>L</math> tensor where <math>L \le M</math>.

=== Coordinate representation ===
The first vector space isomorphism on the list above, <math>V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_M \simeq F^{I_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_M}</math>, gives the [[coordinate vector|coordinate representation]] of an abstract tensor.  Assume that each of the <math>M</math> vector spaces <math>V_m</math> has a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] <math>\{ v_1^m, v_2^m, \ldots, v_{I_m}^m \}</math>.  The expression of a tensor with respect to this basis has the form <math display="block">\mathcal{A} = \sum_{i_1=1}^{I_1}\ldots\sum_{i_M=1}^{I_M} a_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_M} v_{i_1}^1 \otimes v_{i_2}^2 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{i_M}^{M},</math> where the coefficients <math>a_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_M}</math> are elements of <math>F</math>. The coordinate representation of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is <math display="block">\sum_{i_1=1}^{I_1}\ldots\sum_{i_M=1}^{I_M} a_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_M} \mathbf{e}_{i_1}^1 \otimes \mathbf{e}_{i_2}^2 \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbf{e}_{i_M}^M,</math>where <math>\mathbf{e}_{i}^m</math> is the <math>i^\text{th}</math> [[Standard basis|standard basis vector]] of <math>F^{I_m}</math>.  This can be regarded as a ''M''-way array whose elements are the coefficients <math>a_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_M}</math>.

=== General flattenings ===
For any permutation <math>\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_M</math> there is a [[canonical isomorphism]] between the two tensor products of vector spaces <math>V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_M</math> and <math>V_{\pi(1)} \otimes V_{\pi(2)} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{\pi(M)}</math>.  Parentheses are usually omitted from such products due to the [[Tensor product#Universal property|natural isomorphism]] between <math>V_i\otimes(V_j\otimes V_k)</math> and <math>(V_i\otimes V_j)\otimes V_k</math>, but may, of course, be reintroduced to emphasize a particular grouping of factors.  In the grouping,
<math display="block">(V_{\pi(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{\pi(r_1)})\otimes(V_{\pi(r_1+1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{\pi(r_2)})\otimes\cdots\otimes(V_{\pi(r_{L-1}+1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{\pi(r_L)}),</math>
there are <math>L</math> groups with <math>r_l-r_{l-1}</math> factors in the <math>l^\text{th}</math> group (where <math>r_0=0</math> and <math>r_L=M</math>).

Letting <math>S_l=(\pi(r_{l-1}+1),\pi(r_{l-1}+2),\ldots,\pi(r_l))</math> for each <math>l</math> satisfying <math>1\le l\le L</math>, an <math> (S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_L)</math>-flattening of a tensor <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, denoted <math>\mathcal{A}_{(S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_L)}</math>, is obtained by applying the two processes above within each of the <math>L</math> groups of factors.  That is, the coordinate representation of the <math>l^\text{th}</math> group of factors is obtained using the isomorphism <math>(V_{\pi(r_{l-1}+1)} \otimes V_{\pi(r_{l-1}+2)} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{\pi(r_l)})\simeq(F^{I_{\pi(r_{l-1}+1)}}\otimes F^{I_{\pi(r_{l-1}+2)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes F^{I_{\pi(r_l)}})</math>, which requires specifying bases for all of the vector spaces <math>V_k</math>.  The result is then vectorized using a bijection <math>\mu_l:[I_{\pi(r_{l-1}+1)}]\times[I_{\pi(r_{l-1}+2)}]\times\cdots\times[I_{\pi(r_l)}]\to[I_{S_l}]</math> to obtain an element of <math>F^{I_{S_l}}</math>, where <math display="inline">I_{S_l} := \prod_{i=r_{l-1}+1}^{r_l} I_{\pi(i)}</math>, the product of the dimensions of the vector spaces in the <math>l^\text{th}</math> group of factors.  The result of applying these isomorphisms within each group of factors is an element of <math>
F^{I_{S_1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_{S_L}}</math>, which is a tensor of order <math>L</math>.

=== Vectorization ===
By means of a bijective map <math>
\mu : [I_1] \times \cdots \times [I_M] \to [I_1\cdots I_M] </math>, a vector space isomorphism between <math>
F^{I_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_M} </math> and <math> F^{I_1 \cdots I_M} </math> is constructed via the [[Function (mathematics)|mapping]] <math> \mathbf{e}_{i_1}^1 \otimes \cdots \mathbf{e}_{i_m}^m \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbf{e}_{i_M}^M \mapsto \mathbf{e}_{\mu(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_M)}, </math> where for every natural number <math>i</math> such that <math>1 \le i \le I_1 \cdots I_M</math>, the vector <math>
\mathbf{e}_i </math> denotes the ''i''th standard basis vector of <math>
F^{i_1 \cdots i_M} </math>.  In such a reshaping, the tensor is simply interpreted as a [[Vector space|vector]] in <math>
F^{I_1 \cdots I_M}</math>.  This is known as '''vectorization''', and is analogous to [[vectorization (mathematics)|vectorization of matrices]].  A standard choice of bijection <math>\mu</math> is such that

<math  display="block">\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal{A}) = \begin{bmatrix} a_{1,1,\ldots,1} & a_{2,1,\ldots,1} & \cdots & a_{n_1,1,\ldots,1} & a_{1,2,1,\ldots,1} & \cdots & a_{I_1,I_2,\ldots,I_M} \end{bmatrix}^T,</math>

which is consistent with the way in which the colon operator in [[Matlab]] and [[GNU Octave]] reshapes a higher-order tensor into a vector.  In general, the vectorization of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is the vector <math> [ a_{\mu^{-1}(i)} ]_{i=1}^{I_1 \cdots I_M} </math>.

The vectorization of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> denoted with <math>vec(\mathcal{A})</math> or <math>\mathcal{A}_{[:]}</math> is an <math>[S_1,S_2]</math>-reshaping where <math>S_1 = (1,2,\ldots,M)</math> and <math>S_2=\empty</math>.

=== Mode-''m'' Flattening / Mode-''m'' Matrixization===
Let <math>\mathcal{A} \in F^{I_1} \otimes F^{I_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{I_M}</math> be the coordinate representation of an abstract tensor with respect to a basis.
'''Mode-''m'' matrixizing''' (a.k.a. ''flattening'') of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is an <math>
[S_1, S_2]</math>-reshaping in which <math>
S_1 = (m)</math> and <math>
S_2 = (1,2,\ldots,m-1,m+1,\ldots,M)</math>. Usually, a standard matrixizing is denoted by

<math  display="block">{\mathbf A}_{[m]} = \mathcal{A}_{[S_1,S_2]} </math>

This reshaping is sometimes called '''matrixizing''', '''matricizing''', '''flattening''' or '''unfolding''' in the literature. A standard choice for the bijections <math>\mu_1,\ \mu_2</math> is the one that is consistent with the reshape [[Function (mathematics)#In computer science|function]] in Matlab and GNU Octave, namely

<math  display="block">{\mathbf A}_{[m]} := \begin{bmatrix} 
a_{1,1,\ldots,1,1,1,\ldots,1} & a_{2,1,\ldots,1,1,1,\ldots,1} & \cdots & a_{I_1,I_2,\ldots,I_{m-1},1,I_{m+1},\ldots,I_M} \\
a_{1,1,\ldots,1,2,1,\ldots,1} & a_{2,1,\ldots,1,2,1,\ldots,1} & \cdots & a_{I_1,I_2,\ldots,I_{m-1},2,I_{m+1},\ldots,I_M} \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
a_{1,1,\ldots,1,I_m,1,\ldots,1} & a_{2,1,\ldots,1,I_m,1,\ldots,1} & \cdots & a_{I_1,I_2,\ldots,I_{m-1},I_m,I_{m+1},\ldots,I_M}
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

Definition '''Mode-''m'' Matrixizing:'''<ref name="Vasilescu2009">{{citation
 |last = Vasilescu |first = M. Alex O.
 |title = Multilinear (Tensor) Algebraic Framework for Computer Graphics, Computer Vision and Machine Learning
 |date = 2009
 |url = https://tspace.library.utoronto.ca/bitstream/1807/65327/11/Vasilescu_M_Alex_O_200911_PhD_thesis.pdf
 |work = University of Toronto
 |page = 21}}</ref>
<math display="block">[{\mathbf A}_{[m]}]_{jk} = a_{i_1\dots i_m\dots i_M}, \;\; \text{ where } j = i_m \text{ and } k=1+\sum_{n=0\atop n\neq m}^M(i_n - 1) \prod_{l=0\atop l\neq m}^{n-1} I_l.</math>
The mode-''m'' matrixizing of a tensor <math>{\mathcal A} \in F^{I_1\times...I_M},</math> is defined as the matrix <math>{\mathbf A}_{[m]} \in F^{I_m \times (I_1 \dots I_{m-1} I_{m+1} \dots I_M)}</math>. As the parenthetical ordering indicates, the mode-''m'' column vectors are arranged by
sweeping all the other mode indices through their ranges,
with smaller mode indexes varying more rapidly than larger ones; thus
